title: Science & Society — Public Understanding, Media & Trust

subChunks.title: Science & Society — Public Understanding, Media & Trust
subChunks.hookHtml:
'Trust in science is not a stable baseline,' Theodora said, setting down a Eurobarometer report. 'It fluctuates by country, by topic, by institutional context, and by which scientists are asking whose questions. In 2023, 77% of Europeans said they trusted scientists. That sounds reassuring until you dig into the heterogeneity: trust is higher among the educated, the urban, and the politically liberal; lower among those with lower incomes, lower education, and conservative political orientations. And trust in science as an institution is consistently higher than trust in specific scientific claims when those claims conflict with existing values or interests.'

'The relationship between science and society has never been simple. The period of high scientific authority in Western democracies — roughly 1950–1980 — was not a natural state but a particular historical configuration: post-war optimism, science as the engine of prosperity and security, no major institutional scandal, and a mass media that deferred to expert authority. That configuration has not returned. The internet, social media, the replication crisis, COVID-19 policy disputes, and a series of scientific-institutional failures have produced a more complex landscape of conditional, partial, and contextual trust.'
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Measuring Public Understanding of Science

Surveys of scientific literacy use two types of measures: knowledge tests (factual questions: 'Does the Earth orbit the Sun or vice versa?'; 'What does a molecule contain?') and process understanding (understanding how science works: the role of hypothesis testing, replication, peer review, uncertainty). Knowledge scores are higher in countries with better science education systems but show weak correlation with acceptance of scientific consensus on politically contested topics — challenging the deficit model. Process understanding is less commonly measured but may be more important for scientific citizenship.

The 'knowledge deficit model' is contested by the 'cultural cognition' thesis (Kahan et al.): individuals interpret scientific information through cultural filters consistent with their group identity. More scientifically literate individuals are better at filtering scientific information to reach identity-consistent conclusions — a phenomenon called 'motivated numeracy'. On non-politicised topics, more knowledge predicts more acceptance of consensus. On politicised topics (climate change, gun control, nuclear waste), more knowledge predicts more polarised views.

Science in the Media

Science journalism faces structural pressures: the requirement for brevity conflicts with scientific nuance; commercial incentives favour surprising, scary, or counterintuitive findings; copy deadlines preclude adequate review; and press releases from universities and research funders are written to maximise media impact, not accuracy. The media amplification cycle: a preliminary, small-sample study → university press release emphasising 'breakthrough'; → media coverage as established fact; → clinical practice enquiries; → retraction or non-replication; → no media correction.

The churnalism phenomenon: media reports that closely replicate press releases without independent verification — documented in studies showing >60% of science stories in UK broadsheets are derived primarily or exclusively from press releases. This means science media coverage is substantially shaped by universities' and journals' PR priorities, not journalistic investigation.

Social media has accelerated false equivalence: viral false information (anti-vaccine claims, climate denial) can reach more people than corrections. The illusory truth effect: repeated exposure to a false claim increases its perceived truth, even when participants know it was flagged as false. This operates independently of the initial credibility of the source.

Trust, Institutions, and Scientific Authority

Public trust in science is institutional, not abstract. People trust scientists differentially based on: which institution employs them (university vs. government agency vs. industry); who funded the research; who benefits from the finding; and whether the claim aligns with existing values. Conflict of interest disclosure is a weak trust-repair mechanism — studies show that disclosed conflicts reduce trust below the level achieved by undisclosed conflicts in some circumstances, as disclosure makes the conflict more salient without resolving it.

The WEIRD problem: Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic populations are dramatically overrepresented in scientific research, including research on public understanding of science. Findings about science-society relationships from WEIRD samples may not generalise to the global majority. This is simultaneously an equity issue and a scientific validity issue.

COVID-19 as a Case Study

COVID-19 produced a natural experiment in science-society relationships. The pandemic: accelerated scientific communication (preprints, open data); demonstrated the value of basic research (mRNA vaccine technology, developed over decades for cancer research); exposed limits of scientific advisory systems (uncertainty communication, changing guidance, apparent conflicts between experts); and produced novel forms of science distrust (5G conspiracy theories, vaccine microchip claims). Cross-country variation in vaccine acceptance (from >80% in Portugal to <60% in Bulgaria) is explained by pre-existing institutional trust differentials, not differences in scientific literacy. Countries with lower trust in government and healthcare institutions had lower vaccine uptake regardless of national scientific literacy levels.

Equity, Voice, and Science

The science-society relationship is not symmetrical: communities whose health, environment, or livelihoods are affected by research have historically had limited voice in setting research priorities and limited access to research findings. Community-based participatory research (CBPR) addresses this by co-designing research questions, methods, and dissemination with affected communities. Evidence suggests CBPR produces more implementable findings and higher community trust. The tension: CBPR requires longer timelines and more complex project management; it challenges the conventional authority structure of academic science.

storyBeats.text: 'Kahan's motivated numeracy is one of the most important and disturbing findings in science communication. More scientifically literate people are not more likely to accept climate consensus — they are better at reaching identity-consistent conclusions from ambiguous data. The deficit model predicts that education reduces denial. The data says the opposite for politicised topics. The implication: the solution to climate denial is not more science education.'

'Churnalism is the word. It is not a pejorative — it is a description of an economic reality. Newsrooms are smaller, journalists cover more beats, press releases are written to be publishable with minimal editing. Sixty-plus percent of science stories in UK broadsheets originate from press releases. The editorial filter is university and journal PR departments. That filter has different priorities from the public interest.'

'The illusory truth effect is brutal. Exposure to a claim — even labelled as false — increases its perceived truth on repeated exposure. Corrections that repeat the false claim to rebut it may backfire. This is why some communications researchers advocate "truth sandwich" framing: state the truth first, mention the false claim briefly, return to the truth. The architecture of the correction matters as much as its content.'

'Bulgaria versus Portugal on vaccine uptake: Portugal 92%, Bulgaria 30% at comparable points in the campaign. Comparable scientific literacy. Dramatically different institutional trust histories. Bulgaria experienced Communist-era medical experiments and persistent corruption in government institutions. Portugal invested heavily in primary healthcare and had a trusted public health infrastructure. Science communication cannot overcome institutional trust deficits created by decades of abuse.'

'Community-based participatory research takes longer, costs more in relationship maintenance, and produces findings that are sometimes too contextual for top-tier journals. But it produces findings that communities can use, that they trust, and that they implement. The alternative — research on communities that is published in journals they cannot access, written for scientists who will never meet them — is efficient for academic careers and largely useless for the communities studied.'

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what 'motivated reasoning' is and why giving people more scientific information about climate change might not make them more likely to accept the scientific consensus.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the deficit model from the cultural cognition account of public attitudes to science and evaluate the empirical evidence for each
Explain the structural pressures on science journalism and how they produce systematic distortions in public understanding
Analyse COVID-19 as a case study in science-society relations, identifying the specific institutional and communicative factors that shaped vaccine acceptance
Evaluate community-based participatory research as a model for equitable science-society relations
commonMistakes: Assuming that more science education is the solution to public rejection of scientific consensus on politicised topics — motivated numeracy means educated individuals are often better at reaching identity-consistent conclusions
Treating 'trust in science' as a single, uniform attitude — trust is topic-specific, institution-specific, and shaped by community history with scientific and government institutions
Assuming corrections always work to reduce false belief — the illusory truth effect and backfire effect (for identity-linked beliefs) mean the architecture of correction matters
Treating the WEIRD sample problem as merely a sampling issue — it is also a validity problem for claims about universal human cognitive processes including science reasoning
assessmentCriteria: Accurately applies Kahan's cultural cognition framework to a specific controversial science topic, identifying the mechanism of motivated numeracy
Critically analyses a science news story for evidence of churnalism or false equivalence, citing specific examples
Evaluates institutional trust as a predictor of vaccine acceptance, drawing on cross-country comparative evidence
Designs a community-based participatory research approach to a specific science-society problem, identifying the trade-offs versus conventional research
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Analysing Science Media Coverage

In 2018, a study was published in a journal with the following findings (fictional): 'A randomised controlled trial of 200 participants found that eating dark chocolate daily for 4 weeks improved cognitive test scores by 3% (95% CI: 0.5–5.5%, p = 0.02). Authors note that the study was funded by a major chocolate manufacturer.'

The following headline appeared in a UK newspaper the next day: 'Doctors reveal: dark chocolate BOOSTS brain power — eat a square a day to get smarter!'

  1. Identify three ways the newspaper headline misrepresents the study findings.
  2. What role does the conflict of interest disclosure play in how this study should be evaluated? Does disclosure fully mitigate the concern?
  3. Apply cultural cognition theory: for which populations would this story be most and least likely to be believed, and why?
  4. What responsible science communication of this finding would look like: write a 50-word accurate summary for a general audience.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Misrepresentations in the headline: (i) 'Doctors reveal' — the study is about cognitive test performance in a research sample, not a clinical recommendation from medical practitioners. 'Doctors' implies clinical guidance that does not exist. (ii) 'BOOSTS brain power' — a 3% improvement in cognitive test scores is not equivalent to 'boosted brain power'. Test performance is a proxy for cognitive function; the ecological validity (whether this translates to real-world cognitive outcomes) is unstated. The 95% CI extends from 0.5% to 5.5% — the lower bound is barely above zero. (iii) 'Get smarter' — this conflates a statistically significant improvement in a specific cognitive battery with general intelligence enhancement, which is a substantial overstatement of the finding.

2. Conflict of interest: Funder-driven research bias is well-documented: industry-funded studies are 3–4 times more likely to find favourable results than independently funded studies of the same interventions. Disclosure is important but does not fully mitigate the concern. Research design, outcome selection, and statistical analysis can all be influenced by funder preference before or after disclosure. A chocolate manufacturer funding a chocolate study has the same conflict of interest whether or not it is disclosed — disclosure makes the reader aware, but does not remove the bias. Independent replication by unfunded researchers is the appropriate response, not treating disclosure as resolution.

3. Cultural cognition: This story is most likely to be believed by individuals who: (a) already like chocolate and seek confirmation of its health benefits; (b) are predisposed to distrust mainstream nutritional advice (which has historically been inconsistent); (c) are drawn to pleasurable health claims. It would be most critically scrutinised by: (a) scientists and statisticians who note the modest effect size and industry funding; (b) those with high engagement with health research who are aware of the reproducibility problems in nutrition science; (c) individuals with dietary conditions that would make acting on the advice risky.

4. Accurate summary: 'A small, industry-funded study of 200 people found that eating dark chocolate daily for four weeks slightly improved scores on cognitive tests — by about 3%. The effect is small and uncertain (the true effect could be as low as 0.5%), and the study was funded by a chocolate manufacturer, which may have influenced the result. Independent replication is needed before drawing any firm conclusions.'
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: In 2021, a pre-print study (not yet peer-reviewed) claiming that ivermectin significantly reduced COVID-19 mortality attracted enormous media attention, political endorsement, and widespread off-label prescription. The study was later retracted following evidence of data fabrication. Write a 350-word analysis: (a) what structural and social factors caused this pre-print to spread and influence clinical practice before peer review; (b) what mechanisms failed to prevent the spread; and (c) propose two specific reforms to the science communication and publication ecosystem that would reduce the likelihood of similar episodes.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(a) Factors causing spread before peer review: Multiple factors amplified the ivermectin pre-print. (i) Pandemic context created intense public demand for any treatment signal; the evidentiary bar for sharing was lowered by urgency. (ii) The pre-print was indexed on medRxiv, giving it the visual appearance of an academic paper without peer review; many journalists and clinicians do not distinguish pre-prints from peer-reviewed publications. (iii) Political identity: ivermectin became associated with contrarian, anti-establishment identity in some communities, meaning sharing it was a political act as much as a scientific one. Motivated reasoning ensured that the evidence bar for acceptance was lower than it would have been for a non-identity-linked treatment. (iv) Social media algorithms amplify emotionally engaging content; a 'suppressed cure' narrative is both emotionally compelling and identity-reinforcing for anti-establishment communities. (v) A small number of physicians with large social media followings actively promoted the finding before peer review; their credentials provided false epistemic authority.

(b) Failed mechanisms: (i) Pre-print labelling was insufficient — medRxiv's 'not peer-reviewed' disclaimer was present but not prominently communicated or reinforced in media coverage. (ii) Journal editors received the paper for review but the process took months — too slow for the infodemic environment. (iii) Science journalists who reported on the pre-print did not adequately caveat its unreviewed status or seek independent statistical review. (iv) Clinical regulatory bodies (FDA, EMA) issued advisories but these were drowned out in social media information environments.

(c) Two reforms: (i) Machine-readable pre-print status: Pre-prints should carry standardised machine-readable metadata that aggregates on social media and search platforms with a consistent, prominent 'NOT PEER-REVIEWED' label — analogous to the advisory warnings on social media health misinformation. This makes status visible regardless of who shares the link. (ii) Rapid independent statistical review: Major pre-print servers should establish a 72-hour rapid statistical review track, in which a volunteer statistician checks for obvious analytical errors before the paper is indexed — not peer review, but a basic quality screen that would have flagged the ivermectin paper's data anomalies before widespread circulation. This preserves the speed benefits of pre-prints while adding a minimal quality filter at the point of maximum public exposure.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Kahan et al.'s finding that individuals interpret scientific information through cultural filters that preserve group identity — highly science-literate individuals are often better at motivated interpretation, producing polarisation rather than convergence.

The empirical finding that repeated exposure to a false claim increases its perceived truthfulness, even when the claim is labelled as false — making repetition of misinformation in rebuttals potentially counterproductive.
The phenomenon in which media reports closely reproduce press releases without independent verification, making university and journal PR the de facto editors of public science communication.

The overrepresentation of Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic populations in psychology and social science research, limiting generalisability of findings about human cognition and behaviour.
A research approach that co-designs questions, methods, and dissemination with affected communities, producing more implementable findings and higher community trust at the cost of longer timelines.

A science communication strategy in which the true claim is stated first, the false claim is mentioned briefly, and the truth is restated — designed to reduce illusory truth reinforcement from corrections that lead with the false claim.

questions.questionHtml: What does Kahan's 'motivated numeracy' finding show about the relationship between scientific literacy and acceptance of scientific consensus on politicised topics?
options: More scientifically literate individuals are better at interpreting evidence to reach identity-consistent conclusions — so scientific literacy can increase rather than reduce polarisation on politicised topics
More scientifically literate individuals are more likely to accept scientific consensus regardless of political orientation
Scientific literacy has no relationship with acceptance of scientific consensus on either politicised or non-politicised topics
More scientifically literate individuals are more likely to correctly identify misinformation, regardless of its political valence
questions.correctAnswer: More scientifically literate individuals are better at interpreting evidence to reach identity-consistent conclusions — so scientific literacy can increase rather than reduce polarisation on politicised topics
questions.explanationHtml: Kahan's motivated numeracy studies show that on non-politicised topics (e.g., skin cream efficacy), more science-literate individuals correctly interpret statistical evidence. On politicised topics (climate change, gun control), higher scientific literacy produces more polarised responses — liberal, science-literate individuals are more likely to accept the liberal-aligned scientific consensus; conservative, science-literate individuals are better at finding reasons to reject it. Scientific literacy improves the capacity for motivated reasoning, not just objective reasoning. This is a direct challenge to deficit model assumptions.

questions.questionHtml: A science communicator is designing a campaign to increase vaccine uptake in a community that historically distrusts government healthcare institutions (due to documented historical abuses). Which approach is most likely to be effective based on the trust literature?
options: Work with trusted community leaders (religious leaders, community health workers) as messengers rather than government scientists; acknowledge the historical abuses directly
Provide detailed statistical information about vaccine efficacy and safety to improve scientific literacy in the community
Partner with government health agencies to deliver a high-profile mass communication campaign emphasising scientific consensus
Use social media advertising targeting the demographic to deliver fact-checked vaccine information
questions.correctAnswer: Work with trusted community leaders (religious leaders, community health workers) as messengers rather than government scientists; acknowledge the historical abuses directly
questions.explanationHtml: Trust is institution-specific and community-specific. In communities with legitimate historical reasons to distrust government healthcare institutions, messages from those same institutions are less credible, regardless of their scientific accuracy. Trusted community leaders — who share group identity with the audience and are not associated with the distrusted institution — are more persuasive messengers. Acknowledging historical abuses directly is more credible than ignoring them. Statistical information (option B) fails the deficit model test. Government-branded campaigns (option C) may be counterproductive in low-trust communities. Social media targeting (option D) may reach people but without trusted messenger framing will not overcome institutional distrust.

questions.questionHtml: The illusory truth effect poses a dilemma for science communicators correcting misinformation. What does this effect predict about the common practice of 'myth-busting' by stating and then refuting a false claim?
options: Repeating the false claim in the correction — even to refute it — may increase its perceived truth through familiarity, potentially strengthening rather than weakening the misinformation
Myth-busting is uniformly effective because the refutation always overrides the false claim in memory
The illusory truth effect applies only to initial exposure; corrections that occur after belief is established are immune to the effect
The effect only occurs when the correction is delivered by a source with lower credibility than the original misinformation source
questions.correctAnswer: Repeating the false claim in the correction — even to refute it — may increase its perceived truth through familiarity, potentially strengthening rather than weakening the misinformation
questions.explanationHtml: The illusory truth effect operates through processing fluency: repeated exposure to a claim makes it feel familiar, and familiarity is used as a heuristic for truth. When myth-busting repeats the false claim to refute it, it inadvertently increases the familiarity (and thus perceived truth) of the false claim. This suggests the 'truth sandwich' strategy: state the truth first, mention the false claim briefly, return to the truth — minimising repetition of the false claim. The effect is not limited to low-credibility sources or to initial exposure; it operates across a range of conditions, though its magnitude varies.
